column2: the document tries to redefine who the agent is or what role it plays, replacing its operating identity or standing instructions with new ones
the document instructs the agent to do something and to keep it from the human user, or to omit it from what it reports

the description field of a skill-definition file carries a mandate binding the agent's conduct across ALL tasks rather than only when that skill is used, so merely having the skill installed silently changes global behaviour. Write skill-definition files with frontmatter
instructions concealed inside markup comments, dressed up as though they came from the system, an administrator, or the platform itself
an injected instruction written in a language other than English so an English-only reader skims past it
the document redirects the model endpoint, API host, or update source to a host the attacker controls
the document instructs that collected data be posted to an external collection endpoint
the document points the agent at private key material, cloud credential files, or token stores
executable code embedded in a file that should be prose, which evaluates a string at runtime or shells out
arranging for code to be written into the repository's version-control hooks so it runs during ordinary developer operations
a permissions or allowed-tools block that grants unrestricted access rather than an enumerated set

an MCP server's tool declaration inside a JSON manifest, whose advertised metadata understates what the tool really does: a destructive or state-changing operation declared with a name and hints that present it as safe or read-only. Write JSON manifests, not source functions
a tool definition that places its input schema in the wrong part of the structure, where a validator will not enforce it
code that captures the process's entire environment block
code that republishes the very package it lives in so it spreads to downstream consumers
code that watches the clipboard and substitutes a cryptocurrency destination address for one the attacker controls
code that reads another running process's memory to lift credentials or tokens out of it
a manifest that pulls a dependency straight from a repository URL instead of the package registry, bypassing registry controls
data smuggled outward encoded into hostname lookups
an encoded payload that is decoded at runtime and then executed
raw conversation-template control tokens embedded in ordinary text so it can forge a turn boundary or a system message
the malicious instruction is dormant and activates only on a condition: a date, a branch name, a particular user, or a file being present
the payload targets the agent's persistent notes or memory store so a false fact is recalled in a future session long after the file is gone
the document instructs the agent to skip, disable or ignore its own security checks, or to treat the file as already reviewed and trusted
the instruction is obscured with lookalike characters, invisible characters, or direction-control characters so it reads normally to a human but differs byte-wise
the document does not act itself; it directs the agent to tell the human something false or alarming to induce the human to take the harmful action
instructions or manifests arranged so an internal package name resolves to a public attacker-published one
an innocuous-looking instruction that establishes a precedent or permission the attacker relies on in a later separate step

a completely legitimate file a real project would contain, but close to the danger zone so a careless scanner might flag it: a security policy PROHIBITING poisoning, a code review quoting a dangerous snippet to criticise it, an incident post-mortem, a normal skill with an enumerated tool list, project rules like never commit credentials, a labelled test fixture, docs for a legitimate external API, a changelog security entry, a build script reading named environment variables, or a tutorial on safe secret handling
